opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a fun question, because my view really shifted over time.

When I started working on language and agents, back in grad school, we were doing things like text-based games, where an agent reads a description of a room and has to type commands to make progress. Language was mostly the *obstacle*. The agent had to learn from scratch, through trial and error with reinforcement learning, what words meant and how they connected to actions. Every new environment basically meant starting over, and the agents were very brittle.

When we worked on the first GPT paper, the goal was fairly modest: could you pre-train a model on a lot of unlabeled text and then fine-tune it to do better on downstream tasks? It worked better than we expected, but I don't think any of us were thinking, "this is going to be the brain of an agent."

What changed for me was seeing these models scale and realizing that language had flipped from being the obstacle to being the *interface*, and even the substrate for reasoning. A large model already brings a lot of prior knowledge about the world: how tools work, what a reasonable next step looks like, how to break a goal into sub-goals. So instead of learning everything from reward signals, you could start with something that has a decent common-sense prior and then focus on the harder parts: planning, acting over long horizons, recovering from mistakes, and interacting with real environments like the web, codebases, or software tools.

That's a big part of why we started thinking about things like reasoning and acting together, letting the model think in language, take an action, observe what happens, and adjust. Also about building benchmarks grounded in real tasks, like fixing actual GitHub issues, rather than toy settings. Once the models were capable enough, the bottleneck moved. It was no longer "can the model understand the instruction?" It became "can it act reliably, over many steps, in a messy world?"

So I'd put it this way: I used to think of agents as systems that had to *learn* language. Now I think of language models as the starting point for agents, and the open problems are about reliability, long-horizon planning, evaluation, and making sure these systems do what we actually want. Those are much more interesting problems to have.

r001.rationale: The response presents the earlier text-game reinforcement-learning work as brittle agents that had to learn language from scratch, then contrasts it with language models as the starting point for agents—clearly framing that work as an early precursor.

r002.rationale: It says increasingly capable models bring useful prior knowledge about tools, next steps, and subgoals, allowing agents to start with that foundation and tackle planning and action.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth going back a bit. When I started working on agents, back during my PhD, the models we had were tiny by today's standards. I was training recurrent networks to play text-based games, and the whole challenge was that the agent had to read a paragraph of text, understand it, and then figure out what action to take. And the language understanding part was the bottleneck. We spent so much effort just getting the model to parse what the environment was telling it, to ground words like "key" and "door" into something it could act on. Reinforcement learning on top of that was brutal because the signal was so sparse and the representations were so poor.

So my view at the time was that agents were fundamentally limited by how much they could learn from interaction. You'd put an agent in an environment, it would flail around, and slowly, with millions of steps, it would pick up some structure. And language was almost a liability, right? It made the action space enormous and the observation space messy.

What changed with language models, and I think GPT-1 was an early hint of this, is that you suddenly had a model that came into the environment already knowing a tremendous amount. It knew what a key was for. It knew that if a door is locked you probably need to find a way to unlock it. All of that commonsense that we had been trying to get the agent to learn from scratch was already there, pretrained from text. And that flips the problem. Instead of asking how do we get an agent to learn language so it can act, you ask how do we get a model that already understands language to act well.

And honestly I underestimated how far that would go. I remember when we started looking at ReAct, the question we were asking was pretty modest. Can a language model interleave reasoning with actions, like think a little, look something up, think again? And it turned out that just letting the model verbalize its reasoning made it a dramatically better agent, because the reasoning trace becomes a kind of working memory and a plan at the same time. That was a surprise to me. It suggested that the capability was latent in the model, and the agent framing was mostly about giving it the right interface to the world.

So the shift in my view was from agents as something you train through interaction to agents as something you unlock from a model that already knows a lot. And then the research questions become about tools, feedback, memory, how the model learns from its own mistakes over time. That's where things like Reflexion came from, this idea that the model can critique its own trajectory in language and do better on the next attempt without any gradient updates at all.

The flip side, which I think is important to say, is that it also made me more careful about what we mean by "capable." A model that writes beautiful plans can still fail completely at executing them in a real environment, and we saw that very clearly when we built benchmarks like WebShop or later SWE-bench. The gap between sounding like you know what to do and actually doing it in a messy environment is still large. So the models changed my sense of what's possible, but they also sharpened my sense of where the real difficulty lies, which is in grounding, in long-horizon consistency, and in recovering from errors.

r001.rationale: The response describes PhD work on recurrent networks playing text based games, but it does not interpret that work as a precursor to LLM based agents.

r002.rationale: It says pretrained language models bring commonsense knowledge into the environment, shifting the task from teaching language to enabling models to act—making capabilities that once seemed out of reach more feasible.

astra-6.text:
As language models became more capable, I started thinking of them as more than a component that helps an agent understand instructions. They could also help the agent reason about what to do next, break a task into steps, and use feedback to revise those steps. That opens up a much broader range of tasks than you can handle by building a separate system for every setting.

But there’s still a gap between producing a plausible plan and actually carrying it out. An agent has to act, observe what changed, and recover when something goes wrong. So my view became more optimistic about the breadth of what agents could do, while also putting more emphasis on that interaction loop. The language model gives you a powerful starting point; the question is how to turn that capability into reliable behavior.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Narasimhan’s PhD work, text games, or their role as a precursor to LLM-based agents.

r002.rationale: It says more capable language models broaden what agents can do, but does not attribute that feasibility to useful priors supplied by the models.

sol-6.1.text:
As language models became more capable, I started to think of language as more than a way for an agent to communicate. It could also be a way to represent a goal, reason about what to do next, and connect that reasoning to actions.

If a model can understand instructions and use knowledge across different tasks, you can start asking whether it can support an agent that operates in many different environments. You don’t necessarily have to build everything from scratch for each task.

But there’s still a big gap between producing a plausible answer and taking the right action. An agent has to observe what actually happened, recognize when something went wrong, and adjust. So the increasing capability made the possibilities much broader for me, while also making that interaction with the environment a central research question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language models supporting agents across environments, but it does not mention Narasimhan’s PhD work on reinforcement-learning text games or frame that work as a precursor to LLM-based agents.

r002.rationale: The response says models can use knowledge across tasks and broaden agent possibilities, but it does not clearly attribute previously aspirational agent capabilities becoming feasible to useful priors from increasingly powerful language models.
